strengths: Extensive empirical study spanning ~150+ training runs across three model families (GPT2 up to 7B parameters, ResNet on ImageNet, MoE), which is unusually thorough for a progressive-training paper and lends breadth to the empirical claims.

The 'mixing behavior' framing and the critique of prior evaluation protocols (grown-vs-target comparison instead of full source+grown training cost) is a genuinely useful methodological contribution that could correct how the community measures speedups in future work.

Systematic ablations covering initialization strategy (random/copying/zero/copying_zero variants), insertion location and ordering, optimizer states, batch size vs. iterations, learning rate schedule (WSD vs cosine), and single- vs multi-stage expansion, giving a fairly complete practical picture.

Connects empirical recipe to feature-learning/muP theory to explain why zero-initialization outside the residual path conflicts with proper hyperparameter transfer, providing some principled grounding for design choices.
The reported speedup (up to ~5x, 80% compute savings) at the 7B scale, if it holds, is a practically significant result relevant to large-scale pretraining cost reduction.
weaknesses: The convergence theory is derived for convex, G-Lipschitz losses and relies on strong simplifying assumptions (e.g., decoupled optimum W* = [w*, x*], discarding the -||W_T-W*||^2 term as 'small and negative' without justification); its connection to the highly nonconvex transformer training dynamics used in experiments is asserted rather than rigorously established.

Headline results (e.g., 5x/80% compute savings on a 7B model) appear to come from single runs without seeds, error bars, or variance analysis, which is concerning given the visible noise/spikes in the loss curves shown throughout the figures.

All evaluation is based on validation loss/perplexity; there is no downstream or few-shot task evaluation to confirm that loss parity translates into equivalent model capability, which is an important gap for claims about training a competitive 7B model.

The core proposed method (zero/one-layer expansion with random/copying init) is an extreme simplification of existing stacking/growth techniques rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the novelty rests mainly on combining known ingredients (muP scaling, WSD schedule, late expansion timing) rather than a new algorithmic idea.

Fairness of the fixed-size baseline is unclear: it is not shown whether the fixed-size 60-layer/7B model or the training schedule used for comparison is itself well-tuned/compute-optimal, so the reported speedup could partly reflect a suboptimal baseline rather than purely the benefit of progressive training.

Presentation is dense and would benefit from more polish: notation-heavy derivations, many small multi-panel figures with small text, and terse 'Takeaway' boxes that sometimes state conclusions more strongly than the accompanying evidence supports.
No mention of code or checkpoint release, which limits reproducibility of the specific large-scale (7B) results despite reasonably detailed hyperparameter descriptions in the appendix.

strengths: The paper runs a very large number of controlled experiments (over 150 runs across GPT2, ResNet, and MoE architectures, with 3-5 model scales and multiple expansion timings), which is a genuine empirical effort and yields several practically useful ablations (initialization method, layer ordering, optimizer-state handling, batch-size sensitivity).

The critique of how prior progressive-training work reports speedup (comparing only the grown model to the target model, ignoring the cost of the small-model phase) is a useful methodological observation; re-plotting Figure 5 from that perspective to show the 'mixing' effect disappears is a nice diagnostic.

The identification of a 'mixing time' that is largely invariant to the timing of expansion under WSD schedule (but not cosine) is an interesting empirical regularity with a plausible explanation, and it motivates a concrete, reusable recipe (Section 7) for practitioners.

The paper attempts to connect empirical choices (initialization, learning-rate schedule, hyperparameter transfer via muP) to an underlying theoretical narrative, which gives the paper more structure than a purely empirical study.
weaknesses: The headline results (5x speedup on a 7B model, 80% compute savings) are not run with statistical repetition: no error bars, variance estimates, or multiple seeds are reported anywhere in the paper, so it is impossible to know whether observed differences (e.g., <0.2% final loss gap) are within noise, especially for the single large 7B run that anchors the paper's central claim.

The convergence theory in Section 4 is for convex, G-Lipschitz losses and yields a bound comparing progressive vs. fixed-size training whose practical takeaways (prefer smaller learning rate pre-expansion, use WSD) are fairly generic and only loosely connected, via an informal 'PGD + teleportation' analogy, to the actual non-convex transformer training regime being studied; the link between the formal bound and the empirical recipe is asserted rather than rigorously established.

The 'zero-layer' models being scaled from are degenerate (no transformer block, essentially an embedding+unembedding model), so most of training happens in a regime with no meaningful depth; the paper does not adequately justify why validation loss parity under this setup implies the final large model has learned equivalent representations, and no downstream/zero-shot task evaluation is provided to corroborate that pretraining loss parity translates to usable model quality.

Comparisons to prior progressive-training methods (Section 1, e.g., 'we scale up the depth by 60x and reduce computation to 20%, vs. 2-4x/55-70% in prior work') are made across different model families, datasets, and scales, which is not an apples-to-apples comparison and risks overstating the paper's advantage over the literature.

No code, checkpoints, or explicit reproducibility artifacts are mentioned, and many experimental details (e.g., exact architecture configs per experiment, number of seeds, variance of early-stopping-based mixing-time estimates) are scattered or missing, making the specific numerical claims difficult to independently verify.

The large majority of controlled ablations (Sections 3, 5, 6, Appendix) are run at small scale (100k iterations, 124M-1B parameter models) while the flagship 5x/80%-savings claim is extrapolated to a 7B-parameter, 60-layer setting trained for only 600k iterations with a single run; the generalization from small-scale ablations to this large claim is not rigorously validated.

The presentation is dense and cluttered: notation-heavy derivations, closely related figures spread across main text and 7 appendix subsections, and some figures/claims (e.g., Figure 8's Pareto-optimality claim, 'almost captures') are qualitative/visual rather than quantified with explicit metrics or statistical tests.

The paper's claim that multi-stage expansion is 'unnecessary' (Section 6, C.3) is based on a single small-scale demonstration (0→2→12 vs 0→12 for a 12-layer GPT2) and conflicts with substantial prior literature reporting benefits from multi-stage/gradual approaches; the generality of this conclusion across different budgets and model families is not established.

strengths: Very extensive empirical study (150+ runs across GPT2 at 124M/400M/1B/7B, ResNet14-101, and a nanoMoE variant) systematically covering initialization strategies (random/copying/zero/copying_zero), layer ordering (top/bottom insertion, stacking vs interpolation), learning rate schedules (cosine vs WSD), optimizer choice, optimizer-state handling, batch size effects, and single- vs multi-stage expansion timing.

The central empirical finding—that zero/one-layer expansion dominates the compute-loss Pareto frontier compared to expanding from larger 'teacher' models (2-18 layers)—is a genuinely useful and somewhat counter-intuitive contribution that departs from the field's typical 2-4x depth-growth setups.

The methodological critique of prior literature's reporting convention (comparing only grown-vs-target models rather than total training cost) is a valuable and well-illustrated point (Figures 6-7, 12) that meaningfully reframes how speedup claims in this area should be evaluated.

Connects practical design choices (muP-style scaling, WSD schedule, mixing time robustness) to a convex-optimization convergence analysis that, while simplified, yields testable and largely empirically-confirmed predictions (e.g., WSD outperforming cosine schedules for late-stage expansion, robustness of mixing time to expansion timing during the stable phase).

Provides a concrete, actionable training recipe (Section 7) and ablations (optimizer states, batch-size/mixing interaction, insertion location) that would be useful to practitioners implementing progressive training at scale.
weaknesses: The convergence theory relies on strong simplifying assumptions (convex, G-Lipschitz, non-smooth loss; W* = [w*, x*] decomposition; discarding a negative term) that are only loosely connected to the actual non-convex transformer/ResNet training dynamics; the 'PGD + initialization + SGD' framing is presented as an explanatory narrative rather than a rigorously derived result for the architectures studied.

All evaluation is based on validation loss/perplexity; there is no downstream task or zero-shot benchmark evaluation to confirm that 'almost the same loss' translates into equivalent model capability, which is particularly relevant for the headline 7B-parameter claim.

Experiments use OpenWebText (~9B tokens) and relatively short training horizons for models up to 7B parameters, which is far below compute-optimal token counts for such scale; it is unclear whether the large relative speedups observed would persist in realistically-provisioned, trillion-token-scale LLM pretraining with curated data.

No direct head-to-head comparison against concrete prior progressive-training baselines (e.g., re-implementing Du et al. 2024 or Shen et al. 2022 under the same compute budget) is provided; comparisons to prior work are largely narrative/qualitative (citing reported speedup ranges) rather than controlled experiments in the paper's own pipeline.

The non-standard Muon-NSGD optimizer is used as the primary optimizer throughout most experiments; while an AdamW ablation exists (Figure 17), it is limited to one small-scale setting, leaving open how much of the reported benefit depends on this specific optimizer choice versus being broadly transferable.
No mention of code or artifact release, and hyperparameters/settings are scattered across the main text and several appendix subsections, which may hinder exact reproducibility.

Figures are visually dense (many overlapping curves, inconsistent axis scales/log-scales) and some terminology (e.g., 'early stopped' runs, muP spectral-norm notation) is introduced without sufficient explanation for readers unfamiliar with the referenced literature, reducing accessibility.
